text:
Increased turbidity and siltation in lower Howard Creek would have an adverse impact on the spawning runs of rainbow trout and brown trout that have been observed in the lower 0.5 mile section of this stream. Timmerman, (1976) states that "As of this date [March 25, 1976], Howard Creek is the only tributary in South Carolina which receives a spawning run of trout, a unique and highly desirable feature." Spawning runs in Howard Creek were first documented during the winter of 1975-1976 (Section 2.2.2.2), but spawning may not have been successful. The portions of Howard Creek where these runs of trout were observed presently contain considerable areas of sandy bottom. Sediment from construction activities could make portions of lower Howard Creek unsuitable for trout spawning for at least part of the construction period and for a period of recovery.
The relocation of a portion of Highway 171 would necessitate placing a large quantity of earth fill, an activity that would increase siltation and turbidity in Howard Creek above the project and adversely impact the native trout fishery found there. Measures to control erosion from this source have not been outlined.
Construction of the power tunnel, powerhouse, adits, and discharge structure in the Whitewater Arm of Lake Jocassee would cause increased turbidity in this area. Although a cofferdam would be placed around the area of construction, adverse conditions could still persist in the Whitewater Arm during this time.
Placement of tunnel spoil and disturbance of bottom sediments during construction of the proposed submerged weir would also result in increased turbidity (Exhibit W, Appendix J). Applicant proposes to take corrective measures to localize turbidity should it become excessive. The measures to be taken have not been proposed.
The increase in turbid conditions in portions of Lake Jocassee would result in reductions in light penetration, limiting photosynthesis and the growth of planktonic organisms. Benthic areas would receive some sediment deposition that could reduce the productivity of these areas. The affected portions of the lake could become unsuitable for fish, causing them to move into other parts of the lake for as long as adverse conditions persist.
